A local search strategy starting from Batcher's 48-comparator network, using iterative removal and repositioning of comparators guided by the 0-1 principle, will discover structurally novel 45-comparator networks more efficiently than naive bottom-up synthesis.

Extending the proven optimal 12-input network (39 comparators) by inserting 5 additional comparators involving the 13th channel could yield a 44-comparator 13-input sorting network, beating the known 45-comparator best.

A constructive greedy search strategy that selects the next comparator to maximize the reduction in unsorted 0-1 vectors will discover a sorting network of size 48 for n=13 more reliably under a fixed budget than random topological modifications of Batcher's odd-even mergesort network, and has a nonzero probability of finding a network of size 46 or 45 if equipped with random restarts.

A 13-input sorting network of 44 comparators cannot be constructed by extending an optimal 12-input network (39 comparators) with only 5 integrative comparators, because integrating the 13th channel requires at least 6 new comparators, explaining why search stalls at 45.

Greedy single-comparator removal from Batcher's odd-even mergesort network for n=13 (48 comparators) will get stuck above 45 comparators, discriminating the 'structural barrier' hypothesis (predicts stall >45, meaning 45-nets require fundamentally different structure) from the 'redundant Batcher' hypothesis (predicts reaching ≤45, meaning the best-known 45-net is extractable as a subnetwork of Batcher's construction). The structural barrier hypothesis is expected to be supported.

A 44-comparator 13-input sorting network likely exists and would be discoverable via a 3-way merge decomposition: independently sort subsequences of sizes 4, 4, and 5 (cost 5+5+9=19 comparators), then merge the three sorted runs with a custom 3-way merge costing at most 25 comparators, yielding total ≤ 44. The reason search stalls at 45 is that standard pairwise-merge decompositions (e.g., 6+7 or 12+1) inherently require more merge comparators than a 3-way merge that exploits simultaneous cross-run comparisons.
